pr_title: Resolution: Always prefer truly exact resolution match
pr_body:
## Description

Changes the output resolution choice logic to prefer an exact resolution match in both dimensions over an exact match in only one dimension.

## Motivation and Context

This fixes https://github.com/xbmc/xbmc/issues/19037.

For a real-life example where it matters, see https://github.com/xbmc/xbmc/issues/19037#issuecomment-766551412.

## How Has This Been Tested?

Untested so far.

pr_comments:
What the current code does not do is using width and height information in combination, which is why the 4096x2160 use-case gets broken. Width is out, but height is in, so the "||" combination matches.

In my opinion only perfect matches make sense. Cause if kodi does partially scale e.g. 1536x768 to 1600x1200 and then the TV scales it again to 3840x2160 makes barely sense.

Perhaps we can very highly simplify it and with the whitelist allow further fine tuning.

> In my opinion only perfect matches make sense. Cause if kodi does partially scale e.g. 1536x768 to 1600x1200 and then the TV scales it again to 3840x2160 makes barely sense.

I think I would agree here (and it's in line with this PR). If I correctly understand the case you're describing, it means:

- TV's native resolution is 3840x2160
- content's resolution is 1536x768
- the user has manually whitelisted 1600x1200 which the TV supports as input (and then scales and crops or stretches internally to fill the whole screen)

So yes, I too think Kodi should directly scale the content to 3840x2160 – _unless_ the TV supports 1536x768 input _and_ the user whitelisted that resolution.

> Perhaps we can very highly simplify it and with the whitelist allow further fine tuning.

That would be cool I guess. I think the resulting output resolution "algorithm" then should be separately documented/explained in words and/or pseudo-code to allow future visitors to quickly grasp the keypoints that need to be considered.
Does this work for you: https://paste.ubuntu.com/p/tgDZYTNZ5C/ ?

> Does this work for you: https://paste.ubuntu.com/p/tgDZYTNZ5C/ ?

This patch is equivalent to https://github.com/fritsch/xbmc/commit/69c9eabbff6750242aea78ab6d42ce42619c5f0e, right?

Then – supposed I'm reading the code right – **no**, this wouldn't quite work for me since

1. `pen` evaluates to `0` in the first loop iteration in [L130-L155](https://github.com/fritsch/xbmc/blob/69c9eabbff6750242aea78ab6d42ce42619c5f0e/xbmc/windowing/Resolution.cpp#L130-L155) (because `fabs(info.iScreenHeight - height)` = `fabs(2160-2160)` = `0`)

2. subsequently `pen` is assigned to `penalty`

3. the if-clause in [L146](https://github.com/fritsch/xbmc/blob/69c9eabbff6750242aea78ab6d42ce42619c5f0e/xbmc/windowing/Resolution.cpp#L146) evaluates to `false` in all subsequent iterations since by defintion  `pen >= 0` and thus `(pen < penalty)` (i.e. `(pen < 0)`) will always be `false`.

I assumed that the whitelisted resolutions in `indexList` are in descending order (i.e. 4096x2160, 3840x2160, 1920x1080, ...), meaning during the first loop iteration `info.iScreenHeight=2160` and `info.iScreenWidth=4096`. That's correct, isn't it?
Good catch. Let me change the * with a + and we should be good to go.

The order might be arbitrary, that's why that happens for you. First one matches and then it returns. The change, leaving the multiplication with zero out obviously should check all modes and the choose the one with the best distance, but only in that special case for exact match as I don't want average fit and only using it for candidates.

## Bug report
### Describe the bug
Here is a clear and concise description of what the problem is:
<!--- Provide a more detailed introduction to the issue itself, and why you consider it to be a bug -->

<!--- Put your text below this line -->
When playing a 3840x2160 video on a 3840x2160 display, Kodi switches to 4096x2160.


## Expected Behavior
Here is a clear and concise description of what was expected to happen:
<!--- Tell us what should happen -->
<!--- Put your text below this line -->
Kodi should switch to 3840x2160.


## Actual Behavior
<!--- Tell us what happens instead -->
<!--- Put your text below this line -->
Kodi switches to 4096x2160.


## Possible Fix
<!--- Not obligatory, but suggest a fix or reason for the bug -->
<!--- Put your text below this line -->
https://github.com/xbmc/xbmc/blob/66d5ea75bd3d67a320fcbdca81261381951a7cc8/xbmc/windowing/Resolution.cpp#L134

The above comparison allows 4096x2160 to "exactly" match 3840x2160 because, at evaluation time,
```
height = 2160
width = 3840
info.iScreenHeight = 2160
info.iScreenWidth = 4096
```

The condition will therefore evaluate to true.

comments: Could you name the reason why you have 4096x2160 in your whitelist?
I whitelisted all the modes supported by my hardware.
Only whitelist the modes you want to use.
I want to use 4096x2160 for 4096x2160 videos. I would expect Kodi to match the resolution to the content exactly, not choose the first one that matches its height.

> I want to use 4096x2160 for 4096x2160 videos. I would expect Kodi to match the resolution to the content exactly, not choose the first one that matches its height.

I believe this is the intended behavior. See https://github.com/xbmc/xbmc/pull/14132

Just disable 4096x2160 and let the image be scaled to 3840x2160.

I know this probably seems odd but there is really no 100% solution for all cases.

Thanks for the context. To be clear, I know I can fix the problem by disabling 4096x2160. But, I don't want to just fix my issue and move on, I want to help make this software better for other people.

Reading through the examples in the linked PR - they're talking about an error of a few dozen pixels at most, and only in cases where there is no existing match for the video resolution. What we are dealing with here is Kodi choosing squarely the wrong resolution when an exact match is available. Technical users like ourselves can identify the error and "manually select desired resolution", but how many people are out there unknowingly watching 16:9 content on their 16:9 OLEDs with stretched pixels and vertical bars as a result of this behavior?

To put it another way, would you agree that is logic is strictly better than what we have today:
1. If: an exact resolution and refresh rate are available, choose that
2. Else: fall back to old behavior

I can scrape together a PR that accomplishes this, but I've never contributed to this repo before and I'd rather not waste my time if that contribution is not welcome.

The whitelist really is for users that need to fine tune their resolution switching if the default logic doesn't work for them.

The whitelist was also designed to use lower resolutions to avoid upscaling in shaders and allowing the monitors native scalers to do the work.

Again there really isn't a 100% solid solution here and by changing this behavior likely something else will break.

Kodi will scale the media to whatever resolution is currently being used if the media doesn't match the resolution anyways. So if users want to watch all their media at 1080p60 they are free to do so.

So you are free to make a PR but I cannot say if it will be accepted or not without seeing the solution.

> The whitelist really is for users that need to fine tune their resolution switching if the default logic doesn't work for them.

The default logic fixes the refresh rate which leads to visible stutter in most content. It's why I started using the whitelist.

> Again there really isn't a 100% solid solution here and by changing this behavior likely something else will break.

I'm not advocating for a 100% solution, I'm advocating for choosing the exact resolution from the whitelist if one is available. I can't imagine why any user would want Kodi to choose the wrong whitelisted resolution over the exact match whitelisted resolution.

I can't help but feel like the response is just defending the existing logic and not considering my argument on its merits.
Simply create that PR and let's discuss possible solutions on existing (proposed) code.

I support what @vboginskey described.

My particular case:

1. I have a display (actually a Sony VPL-VW570ES) with a native resolution of 4096x2160. It displays 3840x2160 input signals pixel-perfect, too (by leaving a width of 256 pixels blank, 128 on each side). I want the display instead of Kodi to perform the upscaling whenever possible, so I whitelisted all available resolutions.

2. I get some weird resolution choices by Kodi:

    1. **For media in 3840x2160 Kodi chooses an output resolution of 4096x2160.** -> Doesn't make any sense to me since the media's resolution would either need to be cropped in height or otherwise need to be stretched in width (changing the aspect ratio) in order to fit in the output resolution of 4096x2160.
    
    2. **For media in 3840x1604 Kodi chooses an output resolution of 3840x2160.** -> Ok, but suboptimal depending on your preference since the media could be scaled proportionally to the max output resolution of 4096x2160 (i.e. without affecting the media's aspect ratio).
    
After studying `xbmc/xbmc/windowing/Resolution.cpp` I think the logic in there is somewhat skewed.

The `<=`s in the following if-condition do simply not differentiate between an _exact_ resolution match of media and output (2D resolution congruence) and a media resolution that just "fits in" the output resolution by exactly matching only one of width or height (1D resolution congruence):

https://github.com/xbmc/xbmc/blob/66d5ea75bd3d67a320fcbdca81261381951a7cc8/xbmc/windowing/Resolution.cpp#L134-L135

Therefore I've submitted https://github.com/xbmc/xbmc/pull/19119 fixing the first case of the two I described above. I'd be glad if you could test it since I don't really want to get into building Kodi myself.

The second case could also be tackled of course but I believe this would only make sense in combination with giving the user more control (i.e. introducing another display option in the settings), as some people might prefer to see some unused space on their displays instead of Kodi scaling the input media.

Fix it. Send a Pull Request. Writing walls of text and complaining about flawed logic, has now promoted you to make it better.

So, the world was waiting for you to fix this flawed logic. The stage is yours.

I comments in your PR: https://github.com/xbmc/xbmc/pull/19119/commits/480fc8608417d9d2193cb6ceab8db0d87ed9d7cb#diff-e899258d7761060e9bb26f447566bb60a5f8d7c138565c5260f8bb4ac1b062a1R151 

you broke 1600x800 for example and others ... your logic seems flawed.

Edit: If you check the code you know it's really not so easy to not break other stuff and trust me the encoding out there are in doubt fucked up. And then there are users whitelisting 4096 with their TV while even knowing that this is not the native resolution and are so stubborn to just program it in, while kodi with it's non linear scaling would nicely fit it into 3840.

My point (as also descriped in the PR) says: Don't try to quirk without considering all cases. The Whitelist was done to give users a chance to influence automatisms. Adding a 4096x2160 resolution to a whitelist while the native resolution of the TV is 3840x2160 makes absoluteley zero sense and what you wanted to achieve, e.g. pixel perfect output will be nuts.

If you want to solve it more scientifically, keep in mind: you won't find a solution for every case, there will still be someone complaining.

Quite good examples are "old" 4:3 or similar modes, like 1600x1200 or 1024x768 and 1280x768 - but let's leave them shortly out.

What we could agree on I think is the following:
- If the image matches the width of a resolution while the height of the image still fits into this resolution, it is a nice match. Example: Resolution 1920x1080: 1920x800 and 1920x816 videos should be display there.
- If video file perfectly "matches" into available resolutions, we can save us this discussion. Problems start when things don't directly match, e.g. macroblock widths and width / heights get mixeed. E.g. a silly demuxer tells a h264 video is 1088 in height while it only is 1080. This is where this +8 workaround is coming from ... in the first place.

So: What could one do to get it "better":
- Allow user to add / remove resolutions from the list like it is now
- Change the matching algorithm to be simpler but also more generic. Having 8 loops won't help anywhere.
- Prefer width over height for landscape videos.

So, if you really want to change something, try euclidian distance with width weighted higher (lower value at the end therefore worse penalty term, see * 2 below) than height and choose the minimum.

E.g. 1920x800 input, choose 1920x1080, because: (2 * (1920-1920))^2 + (1080-800)^2 is a better match than (2 * (3840-2160))^2 + (2160-800)^2). 

And even this will get complicated as low resolution width are quite near to each other and will fool your results. Famous example: 2560*1600 - would it choose 3840x2160 oder 1920x1080? :-)

I hope you now understand why tuning has limits.

For above bug report: Plain remove your 4096 resolution from the whitelist. It's idiotic and exactly those special cases will make this code very hard to write and to debug.

Ok, thanks for the detailed explanation, makes sense to me except for one fundamental assumption of yours being wrong in certain cases: Some devices (as the Sony VPL-VW570ES projector in my case) act as they had multiple native resolutions. While the projector panel's full resolution is actually 4096x2160, it also displays 3840x2160 input signals completely pixel-perfect (by leaving blank spaces on the left and right as I described above).

Besides that I'd totally vote for

> Change the matching algorithm to be simpler but also more generic. Having 8 loops won't help anywhere.

But I guess I'm not the right person to do this since I'm neither familiar with the codebase nor proficient in C++...

How do the blank spaces work?

You know, when kodi outputs 3840x2160 on a 4096 x 2160 screen content, it will actually already touch each and every pixel so that you have 4096xsomething output. Picture is broken the very moment you output something to it, pixel data has been altered.

> How do the blank spaces work?

Kinda like letterboxing works, but horizontally. In case of a 3840x2160 input signal, the projector just outputs an image with the same height as with an 4096x2160 input signal _but_ with 256 pixels less width. No scaling, no stretching. With the advantage that the blank space is not just black picture but really dark (i.e. no direct light from the lamp; IDK how exactly this is achieved, I guess some kind of aperture is used).

> You know, when kodi outputs 3840x2160 on a 4096 x 2160 screen content, it will actually already touch each and every pixel so that you have 4096xsomething output.

🤨 I can't quite follow I'm afraid. I think what you're describing is my original concern and the reason why I stumbled upon this issue: I do _not_ want Kodi to output a 4096x2160 signal in case of 3840x2160 content because that would necessarily imply the content either being

1. cropped (bad),

2. changed in aspect ratio (bad) or

3. rendered with vertical blank (black) bars. This seems the best strategy but is a) not done right now AFAICT from my experience and b) still not desirable in my case since these black bars would be illumined by the projector while they aren't illumined with a 3840x2160 output signal.
Cool, then we agree.

review_comments: This makes barely sense again. You would not want a 1600x800 (original for a 4:3 screen) video be played at 1280x800 resolution only cause the height matches ... it's wrong and will worsen current behaviour.

Ok, I see your point. I didn't really intend to change the logic in this regard.
How about now? The only difference should be that truly exact matches (i.e. in both width _and_ height) are preferred over anything else, so the 4:3-case you mentioned should be displayed in the same resolution as before this PR.

It makes basically no sense to Display a 1600 x800 video on a 1280x800 screen right? 

Because of the aspect ratio it would end up being displayed as 1280 x 600 or something. So even the 800 would not match.

I still think to break normal files while fixing a non native resolution in the whitelist is wrong to do. You cannot make it right for every user and especially not those that like shooting in their foot.

My changes as they are right now should not affect the resolution choice in case of "a 1600 x800 video on a 1280x800 screen" and similar situations. It should **only** ensure that it accomodates what @vboginskeyin  proposed in https://github.com/xbmc/xbmc/issues/19037#issuecomment-756558351, i.e.

> To put it another way, would you agree that this logic is strictly better than what we have today:
> 
> 1. If: an exact resolution and refresh rate are available, choose that
> 2. Else: fall back to old behavior

Now, how to implement the above depends on the definition of "exact", of course. This PR is very strict in that regard, i.e. treating only pixel-perfect congruence in both width and height as "exact".
